## Introduction {#sec-apD-intro-en}

@sec-06-why-layers-en gives a web application programmer what they
need to know about computer networks to understand the following
chapter and those that follow it: that communication is organised into
layers, that these layers have names and responsibilities, and that
concepts such as IP, port, MAC or DNS are not loose abstractions, but
concrete pieces of that system. This appendix goes deeper into this
subject beyond what is strictly necessary to develop web applications,
much as a painter does not need to know how to make their own paint to
paint a picture, but benefits from understanding how it is made. Here,
for whoever wants that deeper dive, is the complete formalism of
services and protocols, the exact, field-by-field structure of TCP, IP
and Ethernet headers, and the complete encapsulation process in the OSI
model.

## The Real Protocols per Layer {#sec-apD-protocols-layer-en}

@sec-06-osi-tcpip-en presents the two reference models, OSI and TCP/IP,
and the three TCP/IP layers most relevant to a web programmer. The
following figure brings the two models together, showing how the OSI
layers group into the four TCP/IP layers, and some of the concrete
protocols that run in each: `HTTP`, used by Contraponto, shares the
application layer with `SMTP` (email), `FTP` (file transfer) or `DNS`,
a subject explored further in @sec-06-dns-en; the transport layer is
dominated by `TCP` and `UDP`; and the network layer by `IP`.

![The two models side by side, with the most common protocols in each
layer.](../assets/images/cap06/osi-tcpip-protocolos.png){#fig-apD-osi-tcpip-protocolos-en width="85%"}

## Services and Protocols {#sec-apD-services-protocols-en}

Two concepts are central to understanding, in detail, how layers
communicate with one another: services and protocols.

A **service** represents a set of functions offered to a user by a
provider. That service is made available through **Service Access
Points** (*SAPs*): from the perspective of whoever uses the service, all
of its characteristics are fully defined by the interface at the SAP,
which means the entity providing the service can be treated as
completely abstract, with no need to know how that service is
implemented internally. It is exactly this principle that allows a web
application programmer to use TCP without needing to understand how it
guarantees, internally, the reliable delivery of data.

![On the left, the user of a service exchanges messages with the
provider of that service through a SAP, without knowing its internal
implementation; on the right, the same principle applied to the OSI and
TCP/IP layers.](../assets/images/cap06/servicos-sap-osi.png){#fig-apD-servicos-sap-en width="90%"}

A **protocol**, in turn, is a family of standards for exchanging
information: a set of rules that define the physical connections, the
data formats, the transmission models, and the means used to ensure
correctness against errors and failures in data transmission. While the
service describes *what* a layer offers to the layer above it, the
protocol describes *how* two entities of the same layer, one on the
client side and the other on the server side, communicate with each
other to implement that service.

## The Structure of the Headers {#sec-apD-headers-en}

@sec-06-encapsulation-en explains that each layer adds its own control
information to the data, in a process called encapsulation, and
summarises what each one adds: TCP the ports, IP the addresses, MAC the
physical addresses. It is worth seeing, in detail, the exact structure
of each of these headers, field by field.

### TCP {#sec-apD-tcp-en}

The `TCP` header includes, besides the source and destination ports,
the sequence number and the acknowledgement number:

![The field-by-field structure of a TCP
segment.](../assets/images/cap06/segmento-tcp.png){#fig-apD-segmento-tcp-en width="95%"}

- **Flags**: six single-*bit* indicators, which signal the role of a
  segment in the communication. `SYN` starts a new connection, `FIN`
  ends it in an orderly way, `ACK` signals that the acknowledgement
  field is valid, `RST` abruptly interrupts the connection (typically
  due to an error), `PSH` asks that the data be delivered immediately
  to the application, without waiting to group it with others, and
  `URG` signals urgent data;
- **Window** (*Window Size*): the size of the flow-control window. A
  window is a set of segments that can be sent all at once, for example
  100 segments, without waiting for an individual acknowledgement of
  each one before sending the next. If the receiver takes too long to
  acknowledge receipt, or if the network starts showing signs of
  congestion, the window size is automatically reduced, decreasing the
  sending rate; when the network is free again, the window size
  increases again. In this way, TCP adjusts itself to the network
  conditions at each moment, with no need for the application using it
  to do anything;
- **Checksum**: a value calculated from the content of the segment,
  which lets the receiver detect whether the data was corrupted during
  transmission;
- **Options**: a variable-length field, used by extensions to the TCP
  protocol not provided for in the basic header.

### IP {#sec-apD-ip-en}

The `IP` header includes, besides the source and destination addresses:

![The field-by-field structure of an IP
packet.](../assets/images/cap06/pacote-ip.png){#fig-apD-pacote-ip-en width="95%"}

- **Version**: the IP protocol in use (`4` or `6`);
- **IHL** (*Internet Header Length*): the length of the header itself,
  since it can vary depending on the options present;
- **Total length** of the packet;
- **Identification**: a number used to associate with one another all
  the fragments resulting from the same original packet, when it is
  fragmented;
- **Hop count** (*TTL*, *Time To Live*): the maximum number of hops
  (passes through a *router*) a packet can take before being discarded,
  a safety mechanism to prevent a misrouted packet from circulating
  indefinitely across the network;
- **Fragmentation**: each network has a maximum packet size it can
  carry (the *MTU*, *Maximum Transmission Unit*); if an IP packet
  exceeds that size, it is fragmented into smaller parts, a process
  carried out by intermediate nodes on the network;
- **Protocol**: indicates whether the content of the packet, in its
  data section, is a TCP segment or a UDP datagram, informing the
  transport layer, on the receiving side, how to interpret what
  follows.

### Ethernet {#sec-apD-ethernet-en}

A complete Ethernet frame, under the `IEEE 802.3` standard, has the
following structure:

![The structure of an Ethernet frame, under the IEEE 802.3
standard.](../assets/images/cap06/frame-ethernet.png){#fig-apD-frame-ethernet-en width="100%"}

Besides the destination (`DA`) and source (`SA`) addresses, the frame
includes a **preamble**, a fixed sequence of *bits* that lets receiving
network interfaces synchronise with the start of the transmission; a
**length** field, with the size of the data carried; an **FCS** (*Frame
Check Sequence*), similar in purpose to TCP's *checksum*, which allows
corrupted frames to be detected; and an **interframe gap**, a small
mandatory pause before the next frame can be transmitted.

## Data Reception, in Detail {#sec-apD-reception-en}

@sec-06-encapsulation-en describes, in summary, the reception process:
each layer removes the header that the corresponding layer had added
to it on the sending side, until only the application's original data
remains. In detail, layer by layer: the physical layer detects a signal
with the Ethernet address matching the local network interface, and
passes the information to the link layer; this checks whether the
destination MAC address is its own and, if so, passes the information
to the network layer; this checks whether the destination IP address is
its own and, if so, passes the information to the transport layer; and
this, finally, checks whether there is an application registered on the
indicated destination port and, if so, finally delivers the data to it.

![The reverse path to sending: the signal arrives through the network
card and climbs the layers, one by one, up to the
application.](../assets/images/cap06/rececao-de-dados.png){#fig-apD-rececao-dados-en width="45%"}

## An Overall View {#sec-apD-overview-en}

The same encapsulation and decapsulation principle applies, in even
finer detail, to the complete OSI model, with its seven layers: in
each one, on the sending side, a new header is added (`AH` at the
application layer, `PH` at the presentation layer, `SH` at the session
layer, and so on); on the receiving side, each layer removes the header
that corresponds to it, in a process entirely similar to what was
already seen for TCP/IP, just with more layers involved:

![The complete encapsulation and decapsulation process in the OSI
model, from sender to
receiver.](../assets/images/cap06/encapsulamento-bidirecional.png){#fig-apD-encapsulamento-osi-en width="95%"}

It is worth reviewing, in summary, which address is added by each layer
along this path: the transport layer adds the source and destination
ports, the network layer the source and destination IP addresses, and
the link layer the source and destination MAC addresses, each one
wrapping around the data already prepared by the previous layer:

![The different types of address added at each layer: port
(transport), IP (network) and MAC
(link).](../assets/images/cap06/diferentes-tipos-enderecos.png){#fig-apD-enderecos-camada-en width="85%"}
